Welcome to the team, and let me give you the calendar in two minutes. The weekly call is on Tuesday, at eight in the morning, New York time. It never moves. The methodology review is monthly, on the third Wednesday, and that one moves only if somebody is on a plane. In the last week of every quarter nobody books a new meeting at all. That week belongs to the closing, and if you put something in it you will find it cancelled by Friday. One more rule, and this one is mine: no agenda, no meeting. The agenda goes in the invite, never in a separate message, because the separate message arrives at night and nobody reads it in the morning.

When two people work in different time zones, one of them pays for it, and it is almost always the same one. The person in the earlier zone loses the first hour of the day, because the meetings of the other country land right on top of it. And the first hour is the hour nobody ever gets back. So here is the one thing I tell people to do. Put the hour you do your own work in the calendar, as a real event, with a name. Not a note, not a reminder. An event, so that nobody can book over it. And when somebody asks for a time that does not work for you, remember this: saying no to a time is not saying no to the meeting. Offer another hour in the same sentence, and the conversation ends in ten seconds instead of ten messages.

For an American company, Brazil has one advantage that no country in Asia can offer, and it is the clock. Sao Paulo shares almost the whole working day with New York, and India shares almost none of it. A team in Bangalore starts when New York goes to sleep. A team in Sao Paulo starts one hour earlier and ends one hour earlier, and that is all. The country is also big enough to have more than one time zone inside it, so a company in Sao Paulo and a customer in the north are not always on the same clock, which surprises people who have never worked here. And the advantage has a price. The Brazilian side takes the early meetings and the late ones, because it is the side that can, and over a year that adds up to a lot of mornings.
